skills.name: Describe the effect of heat on nitrates

note.text:
All nitrates decompose on heating, but what is left depends on the metal.
• Sodium and potassium nitrates (very reactive metals) give the nitrite and oxygen:
2NaNO3 → 2NaNO2 + O2.
• Most other metal nitrates give the metal oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen:
2Pb(NO3)2 → 2PbO + 4NO2 + O2. Lead(II) nitrate crackles as it decomposes.
• Silver and mercury nitrates (very unreactive metals) give the metal itself, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen:
2AgNO3 → 2Ag + 2NO2 + O2.
• Ammonium nitrate is not a metal nitrate: it gives dinitrogen oxide and water, NH4NO3 → N2O + 2H2O.
The more reactive the metal, the more stable its nitrate is to heat.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to predict and write equations for what heat does to the nitrate of any metal, and link it to the reactivity series.
Builds on: Lesson {13} (nitrates as the salts of nitric acid) and Form Three the reactivity series.
Leads to: Lesson {15} (the oxides of nitrogen given off) and testing for nitrates.

mistake.wrong: heating sodium nitrate gives sodium oxide and nitrogen dioxide
mistake.right: it gives sodium nitrite and oxygen
mistake.why: Sodium is very reactive, so its nitrate decomposes only as far as the nitrite.

worked_example.problem: Lead(II) nitrate and sodium nitrate are each heated strongly. State what is seen and write the equations.
steps: Lead(II) nitrate crackles, gives off a brown gas and leaves a yellow solid.
Sodium nitrate melts and gives off a colourless gas that relights a glowing splint; the solid left is white.
worked_example.answer: lead nitrate gives {formula('PbO')}, {formula('NO2')} and {formula('O2')}; sodium nitrate gives {formula('NaNO2')} and {formula('O2')}

cards.idea: Sodium and potassium nitrates give the nitrite and oxygen only.
Most other metal nitrates give the oxide, brown {formula('NO2')} and oxygen.
Silver and mercury nitrates leave the metal itself.

pick.q: Two nitrates are heated. One gives off only a colourless gas; the other gives off a brown gas as well. What does this show?
pick.r: The first is the nitrate of a very reactive metal such as sodium or potassium
w: The first is the nitrate of a very unreactive metal
The second has not been heated strongly enough
The two are the same compound
e: An unreactive metal such as silver gives the metal, brown {formula('NO2')} AND oxygen.
Stronger heating would not change which products form.
The same compound would give the same products.
pick.y: Only sodium and potassium nitrates decompose as far as the nitrite, giving off oxygen alone.

pick.q: A nitrate is heated and a shiny solid is left in the tube. Which metal is it likely to be?
e: Sodium nitrate leaves a white nitrite, not a shiny metal.
Copper(II) nitrate leaves black copper(II) oxide.
Zinc nitrate leaves zinc oxide, yellow while hot and white when cold.
pick.y: Only the very unreactive metals, silver and mercury, are left as the metal itself.

pick.q: A nitrate is heated and leaves a solid that is yellow while hot and white when cold. Which oxide is it?
e: Lead(II) oxide is orange while hot and yellow when cold.
Copper(II) oxide is black both hot and cold.
Sodium nitrate leaves a nitrite, not an oxide.
pick.y: Zinc oxide is the one that changes from yellow to white as it cools.

pick.q: Which gas given off when a nitrate is heated would relight a glowing splint?
e: Nitrogen dioxide is brown and would not relight a splint.
Nitrogen puts a splint out.
No carbon dioxide is given off by a nitrate.
pick.y: Every nitrate gives off oxygen on heating, and oxygen relights a glowing splint.

pick.q: What is formed when sodium nitrate is heated?
w: Sodium oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen
e: That is what happens to the nitrates of most other metals, but not to those of sodium and potassium.
Only the nitrates of silver and mercury leave the metal itself.
It does decompose, giving off oxygen.
pick.y: {2}{formula('NaNO3')} → {2}{formula('NaNO2')} + {formula('O2')}: a very reactive metal keeps its nitrogen as a nitrite.

pick.q: What is formed when lead(II) nitrate is heated?
pick.r: Lead(II) oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen
e: Only the nitrates of sodium and potassium give nitrites.
Only silver and mercury nitrates leave the metal itself.
A brown gas and oxygen are given off as well.
pick.y: {2}{formula('Pb(NO3)2')} → {2}{formula('PbO')} + {4}{formula('NO2')} + {formula('O2')}, with crackling and a brown gas.

pick.q: What is formed when silver nitrate is heated?
w: Silver oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen
e: Silver oxide is itself unstable to heat and breaks down to the metal.
Only the very reactive metals give nitrites.
It decomposes readily on heating.
pick.y: {2}{formula('AgNO3')} → {2}Ag + {2}{formula('NO2')} + {formula('O2')}: an unreactive metal is left as the metal.

pick.q: What is formed when ammonium nitrate is heated gently?
e: The salt does not simply split back into its acid and base on gentle heating.
Nitrogen and water come from ammonium NITRITE, not nitrate.
Nitrogen dioxide comes from the nitrates of metals.
pick.y: {formula('NH4NO3')} → {formula('N2O')} + {2}{formula('H2O')}: this is how laughing gas is prepared.

pick.q: Which observation shows that a brown gas given off on heating a nitrate is nitrogen dioxide?
pick.r: It is brown, it turns damp blue litmus red, and it is the only common brown gas here
w: It is brown and turns limewater milky
It is brown and relights a glowing splint
It is brown and smells of rotten eggs
e: Limewater is the test for carbon dioxide, which is colourless.
Oxygen relights a splint, but oxygen is colourless.
Rotten eggs is hydrogen sulphide, which is colourless.
pick.y: {formula('NO2')} is brown and acidic; the oxygen given off with it is what relights a splint.

pick.q: Why do the nitrates of sodium and potassium behave differently from the rest?
pick.r: They are the nitrates of very reactive metals, so they decompose only as far as the nitrite
e: They are nitrates, with the same {formula('NO3')} ion.
Every nitrate contains oxygen.
They do melt, but they also decompose, giving off oxygen.
pick.y: The more reactive the metal, the more stable its compounds are to heat.
Potassium is very reactive, so its nitrate decomposes only as far as the nitrite.
A metal of middling reactivity leaves its oxide, with brown {formula('NO2')} and oxygen given off.
Silver is very unreactive, so even its oxide is unstable and the metal is left.
Zinc is in the middle of the reactivity series, so its nitrate gives the oxide.

questions.prompt: What volume of oxygen, in dm³ at s.t.p., is given off when {n} mol of sodium nitrate decomposes completely?

misconceptions.explain: The equation gives {1} mol of oxygen for every {2} mol of nitrate.
Read the coefficients: {2} nitrate to {1} oxygen.

solution: {2} mol of the nitrate gives {1} mol of oxygen, so {n} mol gives {n} ÷ {2} = {n / 2} mol.

questions.prompt: What mass of lead(II) oxide, in grams, is left when {n} mol of lead(II) nitrate decomposes completely?

misconceptions.explain: The question asks for the mass of the OXIDE left, not of the nitrate.
The ratio is {2} to {2}, that is {1} mol of oxide for each {1} mol of nitrate.

solution: The relative formula mass of {formula('PbO')} is {molarMass('PbO')}.
